transcript:
00:00:02 Samir (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We got about an hour — some buffer — to walk through the edge cases you flagged: very long context windows, high TPS patterns, streaming backpressure and timeouts. Quick intros?
00:00:15 Jordan (Satori - Head of Platform): Hey Samir, Jordan here. Priya, Tom, Anita and Markus are on. We're excited — this is the use case that keeps our infra team up at night.
00:00:30 Priya (ML Eng): Hey all. We're building a real-time recommendations and customer support assistant; the tricky bit is we attach full session history and recent catalog into requests so contexts can hit 100k+ tokens frequently.
00:00:45 Samir: Got it. That's a solid 'long context' example. Lena, do you want to kick off the demo?
00:00:52 Lena (Redwood SE): Yeah, I'll start with the Redwood API flow then jump into Console and Optimize. Note: transcription may mangle a few product names, but we'll try to keep it clear.
00:01:05 Lena: First, long context — our runtime supports KV cache + prefix caching so repeated prefixes don't re-compute. For very large contexts we stream input tokens and maintain a sharded KV cache to avoid reloading entire state.
00:01:25 Tom (CTO): When you say sharded KV cache, is that per-tenant or per-model? We have multi-tenant routing and sometimes mix models for cost reasons.
00:01:35 Lena: Great q. It's per-deployment shard; you can pin cache namespaces per-tenant. For mixed-model routing, we fall back to model-variant-specific caches; there are some compatibility constraints.
00:01:50 Jordan: Compatibility constraints? Like quantized variants won't use the same cache?
00:01:54 Lena: Correct — if you move between FP16 to an int8 quantized variant there is a KV structure change; we do automatic fallback and warm-up but full reuse isn't guaranteed.
00:02:05 Markus (SRE): How does that affect latency on cold starts? Our SLO is 150ms p50 for interactive flows.
00:02:12 Lena: Cold starts can add 100-300ms depending on sequence lengths. We mitigate with pre-warmed pools for Dedicated and with predictive prefetch in our Hosted tier. For Dedicated you can reserve warm instances.
00:02:28 Priya: We're more concerned about sustained 1k+ TPS, not just p50. Does your autoscaler support sustained high TPS with low tail latency?
00:02:36 Noah (Product): We tune autoscaling for throughput patterns — continuous batching and dynamic kernel selection help. But at very high TPS the tradeoff is per-token latency vs cost; that's where Redwood Optimize recommendations come in.
00:02:50 Samir: I'll show a live sim after the API demo: a 1k TPS workload with 60k token average contexts to demonstrate backpressure behavior.
00:03:00 Lena: Jumping into the Console — here is the per-route dashboard, token breakdown, and trace for streaming sessions. We can see when backpressure occurs: request queue length spikes, then we shed non-critical routes or route to a cheaper model variant.
00:03:20 Anita (Infra): When you "shed" routes, that means you return an HTTP 429 or you transparently degrade to a shorter context?
00:03:28 Lena: It depends on policy. You can configure hard-deny (429), prioritize by customer tier, or use graceful degradation: trim oldest context frames or switch to a footprint-optimized model that preserves core accuracy.
00:03:40 Tom: We worry about consistency — trimming context could produce different responses that break downstream logic. Can you do deterministic trimming rules?
00:03:48 Lena: Yes, you can pin a trimming strategy per route: last-n utterances, importance-score based trimming (we provide a cheap scorer), or domain-specific anchors (e.g., keep recent cart state).
00:04:00 Jordan: How do streaming timeouts behave? For example, the client starts a streaming response and the model stalls mid-stream — do you have reconnect semantics?
00:04:09 Lena: We expose streaming heartbeats. If the backend stalls, we send a "partial-response" event with a status and an id. Client can reattach using the request id and get continuation or choose to re-request with prefix cached. There's also server-side automatic retry policies.
00:04:25 Markus: That sounds good, but what's the window for the cache warm-up on reconnects? In practice, we saw retries that double token compute if warm-up misses.
00:04:35 Lena: With warm pools and sticky routing, warm-up is typically sub-second for smaller KV sets; for huge 100k token contexts it can be multiple seconds. This is why we recommend prefix caching and incremental syncs.
00:04:48 Priya: Okay, can you show the API call pattern for streaming with backpressure handling?
00:04:53 Lena: Sure — this is a simplified curl: POST to /v1/generate with streaming=true, include stream_window param and a request_id. We stream events: chunk, heartbeat, partial_status. If client sees high lag, we can negotiate smaller windows or ask the client to switch to chunked poll mode.
00:05:10 Samir: I'm going to start a simulated 1k TPS run now — note that the demo infra is a scaled-down version but will show behavior.
00:05:18 [15:00:00] Speaker 2: background noise, demo in progress
00:05:45 Lena: We're injecting variable context sizes. You can see queue length metrics on the right; at about t+45s we hit a tipping point where latency climbs and we start applying backpressure policies.
00:06:05 Priya: Looks like a lot of retries. Those are client-side retry loops?
00:06:10 Lena: A mix — some are our own internal short retries, others are client retries due to transient 504s. We recommend exponential backoff with jitter; also use our idempotency/request-id to avoid duplicate billing for retries.
00:06:22 Tom: Billing — I assume dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable cost vs hosted consumption?
00:06:28 Samir: Exactly. Dedicated lets you reserve GPU pools and predictable throughput. Hosted is usage-based and can spike costs under 1k+ sustained TPS with huge contexts. We'll surface unit economics in the Optimize tab.
00:06:40 Noah: On Optimize, we run synthetic evals and suggest quantization, batch sizes, and route splits. For example, we may recommend an int8 model for low-criticality paths and keep a FP16 variant for high-fidelity routes.
00:06:54 Jordan: Any concerns about model quality regressions with int8?
00:06:58 Noah: We monitor quality via eval sets and have automatic regression alerts tied to prompt sets. If int8 causes regressions above your threshold, we flag it and roll back or reduce routing percentages.
00:07:10 Priya: Security question — we need SOC 2 and SSO/SAML and KMS. Can we get a private deployment?
00:07:16 Samir: Yes, Private (VPC/on-prem) supports SSO, KMS/HSM integrations and full audit logs. Dedicated gets you isolation but still a Redwood-managed control plane unless you opt for Private.
00:07:30 Anita: For Private, how are security patches handled? We can't be doing manual upgrades across N datacenters.
00:07:36 Samir: We offer an automated update channel for Private with scheduling windows, plus air-gapped hotfixes if needed. We also provide signature-verified packages for on-prem installs.
00:07:47 Jordan: Back to latency: our SLA requirement is p99 under 500ms for support assistant. How realistic is that for 60k+ token contexts at 1k TPS?
00:07:58 Lena: For that profile, p99 500ms is tough. Options: reduce context with importance-based trimming, use prefix-cache aggressively, or move the most latency-sensitive flows to Dedicated pre-warmed lanes with reserved KV memory.
00:08:12 Markus: If we go Dedicated, what is the commit cadence and what flexibility for bursts?
00:08:17 Samir: Dedicated has reserved baseline capacity with burst pools you can enable for short-term spikes. Commit terms are monthly/annual; we can structure a pilot with a month-long trial.
00:08:30 Tom: We need to run our own benchmarks. Can you provide a harness that we can run in our environment?
00:08:35 Lena: Yes — Lena: we'll share the benchmark harness (k6 + our client lib) and suggested config (1k TPS, sequence length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming). It uses the same request-id and heartbeats to emulate production.
00:08:48 Priya: On backpressure, we saw some odd behavior in preliminary tests: streaming connections time out after 45s and our clients didn't have a clean reconnection path. Can we tune streaming timeouts?
00:08:58 Lena: Timeout windows are configurable per-route. We also support on-the-wire keep-alives and chunked heartbeats. If a stream is long-running, recommend a heartbeat interval <15s.
00:09:12 Jordan: What about observability? We need token-level cost breakdown and traceable request ids across services.
00:09:18 Samir: Console provides token-level cost breakdown, per-token latency histogram, and trace integration (OpenTelemetry). We also export logs and metrics to your observability backend.
00:09:30 Anita: Any special networking constraints for Private? We want strict egress control.
00:09:35 Samir: Private supports customer-managed networking, egress control lists, and can be deployed in your VPC with peered subnets.
00:09:44 Priya: Can you run a test where we force a model variant fallback and measure the delta?
00:09:49 Lena: Sure — I'm forcing a model variant switch now; see that tail latency increases by ~120ms during warm-up, CPU and GPU memory jumps while cache warms.
00:10:05 [00:10:05] Speaker 3: (background terminal noise)
00:10:15 Tom: That warm-up is concerning. How do you recommend minimizing warm-up impact for live traffic?
00:10:20 Lena: Two strategies: proactive warm pools for the most critical models and staged rollouts that only switch a small percentage initially. Also, prefix pre-warm from a warm cache snapshot if you can predict traffic.
00:10:34 Jordan: Any guidance on batching versus synchronous low-latency single request paths? We have both types of flows.
00:10:40 Noah: Use hybrid routing: route interactive sessions to latency-optimized lanes (small batch sizes, dedicated instances) and background generation to large-batch lanes. Redwood Optimize can map your traffic mix and propose lane splits.
00:10:55 Priya: Hit me with some numbers — what's a realistic tokens/sec per GPU for your recommended quantized model?
00:11:02 Lena: Roughly — on our latest int8 profile you might see 1.2-2.5 tokens/ms/GPU depending on sequence length and model architecture. For long context there's more KV memory pressure which reduces throughput.
00:11:18 Markus: For contract purposes we need tail-latency guarantees; do you instrument tail latency per-tenant?
00:11:24 Samir: Yes, we provide tenant-level p50/p95/p99 and per-route SLO monitoring; SLA commitments are part of Dedicated enterprise contracts.
00:11:34 Jordan: Okay, I want to outline the PoC success criteria. Priya: can you read them?
00:11:40 Priya: Sure — 1) System sustains 1k TPS with average context 60k tokens for 30 minutes with p95 < 600ms; 2) Streaming sessions reconnect gracefully with no more than 1% duplicate responses; 3) Quality (NDCG for recs) degradation <2% when using recommended quantization.
00:11:58 Samir: That's good. We'll commit to those metrics for a pilot if we can replicate on our infra.
00:12:06 Tom: Last question — data retention and audit logs for compliance?
00:12:10 Samir: You can configure retention per-tenant; Private gives full control. Hosted keeps logs for X days by default but we offer extended retention as an add-on. All logs support export to your SIEM.
00:12:24 Jordan: Great. That's a solid demo.
00:12:28 Lena: Quick recap of artifacts we'll share: 1) benchmark harness link, 2) Dedicated pricing worksheet, 3) security pack (SOC2, SAML, KMS details), 4) sample contract. Links will be emailed.
00:12:40 Samir: Next steps: we'll set up the PoC kickoff for week of Jan 6, Lena will run the 1k TPS bench and send results, Satori will provide prompt set by Friday.
00:12:50 Tom: Thanks, appreciate the depth.
00:12:54 Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll review and circle back.
00:13:00 [Call ends — approximate duration 62 minutes — auto-generated segments omitted in this transcript]
notes: Demo focused on long context (60k-200k tokens), sustained high TPS (1k), streaming backpressure and timeouts
